and

\(U\colon\ell_{1}(H,L_{1}[0,1])\to\left(\bigoplus_{\gamma\in H}L_{1}(B_{\gamma})\right)_{\ell_{1}}\)

such that

\(UV=I_{\bigl(\bigoplus_{\gamma\in H}L_{1}(B_{\gamma})\bigr)_{\ell_{1}}},\)

and a diagonal operator \(D\) on \(\bigl(\bigoplus_{\gamma\in H}L_{1}(B_{\gamma})\bigr)_{\ell_{1}}\) such that

\(\|UP_{H}TJ_{H}V-D\|\leq\varepsilon.\)
Proof.Fold proof

For each \(\gamma\in\Gamma\), define

\(S_{\gamma}=P_{\Gamma\setminus\{\gamma\}}TJ_{\gamma}\colon L_{1}[0,1]\to\ell_{1}(\Gamma\setminus\{\gamma\},L_{1}[0,1]).\)

Apply Lemma 6.3 to \(S_{\gamma}\), with \(\eta=\varepsilon\). We obtain a finite set \(F_{\gamma}\subseteq\Gamma\setminus\{\gamma\}\) and a measurable set \(B_{\gamma}\subseteq[0,1]\) of positive measure such that

\(\|P_{\Gamma\setminus(\{\gamma\}\cup F_{\gamma})}TJ_{\gamma}\jmath_{B_{\gamma}}\|<\varepsilon.\)

By Lemma 6.4, there is a set \(H\subseteq\Gamma\) with \(|H|=|\Gamma|\) such that, for all \(\gamma\in H\), we have

\(F_{\gamma}\cap H=\varnothing.\)

Hence, for every \(\gamma\in H\),

\(\|P_{H\setminus\{\gamma\}}TJ_{\gamma}\jmath_{B_{\gamma}}\|<\varepsilon.\)

Put

\(Y=\left(\bigoplus_{\gamma\in H}L_{1}(B_{\gamma})\right)_{\ell_{1}}.\)

Define \(V\colon Y\to\ell_{1}(H,L_{1}[0,1])\) and \(U\colon\ell_{1}(H,L_{1}[0,1])\to Y\) coordinatewise, for each \(\gamma\in H\), by

\((Vy)_{\gamma}=\jmath_{B_{\gamma}}y_{\gamma},\qquad(Ux)_{\gamma}=M_{B_{\gamma}}x_{\gamma}.\)

Then \(U\) and \(V\) are contractions, and \(UV=I_{Y}\).

Let \(D\colon Y\to Y\) be the diagonal operator given, for each \(\gamma\in H\), by

\((Dy)_{\gamma}=M_{B_{\gamma}}P_{\gamma}TJ_{\gamma}\jmath_{B_{\gamma}}y_{\gamma}.\)

Estimating by columns and using \(F_{\beta}\cap H=\varnothing\), we obtain, for \(y=(y_{\beta})_{\beta\in H}\in Y\),

\(\|(UP_{H}TJ_{H}V-D)y\|\leq\sum_{\beta\in H}\|P_{H\setminus\{\beta\}}TJ_{\beta}\jmath_{B_{\beta}}y_{\beta}\|\leq\varepsilon\|y\|.\)

Therefore

\(\|UP_{H}TJ_{H}V-D\|\leq\varepsilon.\)

∎

Once the operator has been reduced to diagonal form up to a small perturbation, the factorisation argument is the same as in the proof of the main transfer theorems. We first record the corresponding diagonal dichotomy for the localised \(\ell_{1}\)-sum.

(Diagonal dichotomy).

Let \(C\geq 1\), let \(H\) be an uncountable set, and for each \(\alpha\in H\) let \(B_{\alpha}\subseteq[0,1]\) be measurable with positive measure. Suppose that \(L_{1}[0,1]\) has the \(C\)-PFP. Put

\(Y=\left(\bigoplus_{\alpha\in H}L_{1}(B_{\alpha})\right)_{\ell_{1}}.\)

Then, for every diagonal operator \(D\colon Y\to Y\), either \(D\) or \(I_{Y}-D\) factors the identity on \(Y\) with constant \(C\).

Proof.Fold proof

The proof is identical to that of Proposition 5.5, using that each \(L_{1}(B_{\alpha})\) is isometric to \(L_{1}[0,1]\). ∎

We are finally ready for the proof of Theorem 1.6.

Proof of Theorem 1.6.Fold proof

If \(\Gamma\) is finite or countably infinite, the result follows from Corollary 6.2, since \(\ell_{1}(\Gamma,L_{1}[0,1])\) is isomorphic to \(L_{1}[0,1]\). We may therefore suppose that \(\Gamma\) is uncountable.

Let \(C\geq 1\) be such that \(L_{1}[0,1]\) has the \(C\)-PFP, and choose \(\delta>0\) such that \(C\delta<1/2\). Let \(T\colon\ell_{1}(\Gamma,L_{1}[0,1])\to\ell_{1}(\Gamma,L_{1}[0,1])\) be an operator.

Applying Lemma 6.5 with \(\varepsilon=\delta/2\), we obtain a set \(H\subseteq\Gamma\) with \(|H|=|\Gamma|\), measurable sets \(B_{\gamma}\subseteq[0,1]\) of positive measure for \(\gamma\in H\), contractions

\(V\colon Y\to\ell_{1}(H,L_{1}[0,1]),\qquad U\colon\ell_{1}(H,L_{1}[0,1])\to Y,\)

where

\(Y=\left(\bigoplus_{\gamma\in H}L_{1}(B_{\gamma})\right)_{\ell_{1}},\)

such that \(UV=I_{Y}\), and a diagonal operator \(D\colon Y\to Y\) satisfying

\(\|UP_{H}TJ_{H}V-D\|\leq\delta/2<\delta.\)

By Proposition 6.6, either \(D\) or \(I_{Y}-D\) factors the identity on \(Y\) with constant \(C\).

Suppose first that \(D\) factors the identity on \(Y\) with constant \(C\). Since

\(C\|UP_{H}TJ_{H}V-D\|<1/2,\)

Lemma 5.6 implies that \(UP_{H}TJ_{H}V\) factors the identity on \(Y\) with constant \(2C\). Choose an isometric isomorphism

\(W\colon\ell_{1}(\Gamma,L_{1}[0,1])\to Y,\)

which exists because \(|H|=|\Gamma|\) and each \(L_{1}(B_{\gamma})\) is isometric to \(L_{1}[0,1]\). Since \(W\) and \(W^{-1}\) are isometries, it follows that \(T\) factors the identity on \(\ell_{1}(\Gamma,L_{1}[0,1])\) with constant \(2C\).

Suppose instead that \(I_{Y}-D\) factors the identity on \(Y\) with constant \(C\). Since \(UV=I_{Y}\), we have

\(I_{Y}-UP_{H}TJ_{H}V=UP_{H}(I_{\ell_{1}(\Gamma,L_{1}[0,1])}-T)J_{H}V.\)

Moreover,

\(\|UP_{H}(I_{\ell_{1}(\Gamma,L_{1}[0,1])}-T)J_{H}V-(I_{Y}-D)\|<\delta.\)

Thus, arguing as before we conclude that \(I_{\ell_{1}(\Gamma,L_{1}[0,1])}-T\) factors the identity with constant \(2C\), which proves that \(\ell_{1}(\Gamma,L_{1}[0,1])\) has the UPFP.

Lastly, by a classical result , the space \(C[0,1]^{*}\) is isomorphic to \(\ell_{1}(2^{\aleph_{0}},L_{1}[0,1])\). Hence, by the previous argument, \(C[0,1]^{*}\) has the UPFP, and therefore \(C[0,1]^{*}\) is primary. ∎

7.

Final discussion and open questions

−

The spaces \(\ell_{1}\), \(c_{0}\) and \(\ell_{\infty}\), especially the latter, have historically been among the more delicate settings for factorisation and primariness arguments, often requiring arguments different from those used for \(\ell_{p}\), \(1<p<\infty\), or even for sums with respect to arbitrary symmetric bases. Somewhat surprisingly, the methods presented here can only be directly applied in these cases. The reason is that the geometry of \(\ell_{1}\) and of the supremum norm gives enough control over coordinate restrictions to obtain both upper- and lower-triangular reductions.

For \(\ell_{p}\)-sums with \(1<p<\infty\), the situation is less clear. One can often obtain one-sided reductions, either upper or lower triangular, under natural hypotheses, but obtaining both simultaneously seems to require substantially stronger assumptions. This obstruction is not absolute: in , a two-sided reduction was obtained for \(\ell_{p}\)-sums of certain \(C(K)\) spaces. There, the upper-triangular reduction used the \(c_{0}\)-structure of the spaces, while the lower-triangular reduction relied on the special structure of \(C(K)\), in particular on reproducibility properties of \(K\) which force an \(\ell_{1}\)-type behaviour.

It is natural to ask whether there are general hypotheses under which analogous two-sided reductions can be proved for \(\ell_{p}(X)\), \(1<p<\infty\).

Let \(1<p<\infty\). Are there natural and sufficiently broad conditions on a Banach space \(X\) under which the UPFP of \(X\) passes to \(\ell_{p}(X)\)?

In the uncountable setting, the need for a full two-sided reduction can sometimes be avoided. Indeed, once a one-sided finite-interference estimate is available, Hajnal’s free set theorem can remove the finitely many exceptional coordinates on a large subset of the index set. Thus the cotype and self-similarity mechanisms used in the countable reductions above are expected to give corresponding UPFP results for uncountable sums \(\ell_{p}(\Gamma,X)\), \(1<p<\infty\), under the analogous hypotheses.

The PFP and UPFP originate in the study of primariness, so it is natural to ask whether these properties, or primariness itself, are preserved by vector-valued sequence-space constructions.

Is there a Banach space \(X\) with the PFP, respectively the UPFP, such that \(\ell_{p}(X)\), for some \(1\leq p\leq\infty\), or \(c_{0}(X)\) fails the PFP, respectively the UPFP?

Is there a primary Banach space \(X\) such that \(\ell_{p}(X)\), for some \(1\leq p\leq\infty\), or \(c_{0}(X)\) is not primary?

A counterexample to either question would likely have to be rather pathological, while a positive answer seems far beyond the reach of the present methods.

results.statementHtml:
Let \(X\) be a Banach space with the UPFP. Suppose that at least one of the following holds:

  1. (i)

    The space \(X\) is self-similar, in the sense that \(X\simeq\ell_{p}(X)\) for some \(1\leq p\leq\infty\), or \(X\simeq c_{0}(X)\).

  2. (ii)

    The dual space \(X^{*}\) has finite cotype.

Then \(\ell_{1}(X)\) has the UPFP. In particular, \(\ell_{1}(X)\) is primary.

Let \(X\) be a Banach space with the UPFP. Suppose that at least one of the following holds:

  1. (i)

    The space \(X\) is self-similar, in the sense that \(X\simeq\ell_{p}(X)\) for some \(1\leq p<\infty\).

  2. (ii)

    The space \(X\) has finite cotype.

Then both \(c_{0}(X)\) and \(\ell_{\infty}(X)\) have the UPFP. In particular, \(c_{0}(X)\) and \(\ell_{\infty}(X)\) are primary.
The spaces \(\ell_{\infty}(L_{p})\), \(1\leq p<\infty\), and \(c_{0}(L_{1})\) have the UPFP and thus are primary.

Lechner and Speckhofer recently proved a much broader factorisation theorem for Haar system Hardy spaces . In particular, their result also implies the UPFP for \(L_{p}\), \(1\leq p<\infty\), and for \(\ell_{\infty}(L_{p})\) when \(1<p<\infty\). The point of the corollary above is that, once the UPFP of a Banach space X is known, the passage to \(\ell_{\infty}(X)\) follows from the elementary triangular-reduction argument developed here.
For every ordinal \(\alpha\), the space \(\ell_{1}(C(\alpha))\) has the UPFP. In particular, \(\ell_{1}(C(\alpha))\) is primary.
For every set \(\Gamma\), the space \(\ell_{1}(\Gamma,L_{1}[0,1])\) has the UPFP. Consequently, \(C[0,1]^{*}\) has the UPFP and, in particular, is primary.

Let \(T\colon X\to Y\) and \(S\colon Z\to W\) be operators between Banach spaces. We say that \(S\) factors through \(T\) with constant \(C\) if there are operators \(V\colon Z\to X\) and \(U\colon Y\to W\) such that

\(UTV=S\quad\text{and}\quad\|U\|\|V\|\leq C.\)

If such a constant \(C\geq 1\) exists, we simply say that \(S\) factors through \(T\).

Let \(X\) be a Banach space.

  1. (a)

    We say that \(X\) has the primary factorisation property (PFP) if, for every operator \(T\colon X\to X\), the identity operator \(I_{X}\) factors through either \(T\) or \(I_{X}-T\).

  2. (b)

    Let \(C\geq 1\). We say that \(X\) has the \(C\)-primary factorisation property (\(C\)-PFP) if, for every operator \(T\colon X\to X\), the identity operator \(I_{X}\) factors through either \(T\) or \(I_{X}-T\) with constant \(C\).

  3. (c)

    We say that \(X\) has the uniform primary factorisation property (UPFP) if \(X\) has the \(C\)-PFP for some \(C\geq 1\).

Let \(T\colon E(X)\to E(X)\) be an operator with matrix of \((T_{n,m})_{n,m\in\mathbb{N}}\). We define the diagonal part of \(T\) to be the diagonal operator \(D\colon E(X)\to E(X)\) given by

\(D(x_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}=(T_{n,n}x_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}.\)

Equivalently, \(D=\operatorname{diag}(T_{n,n}:n\in\mathbb{N})\).

Let \(T\colon E(X)\to E(X)\) be an operator with matrix of \((T_{n,m})_{n,m\in\mathbb{N}}\). We define the upper triangular part and the lower triangular part of \(T\) to be the linear maps initially defined on \(c_{00}(X)\) by the matrices

\(U_{n,m}=\begin{cases}T_{n,m},&n\leq m,\\ 0,&n>m,\end{cases}\qquad L_{n,m}=\begin{cases}T_{n,m},&n\geq m,\\ 0,&n<m.\end{cases}\)

Throughout the paper, we leave the extension from \(c_{00}(X)\) to \(E(X)\) implicit and focus on the only problematic point, namely the boundedness of the corresponding triangular truncation. Equivalently, one may first regard these truncations as coordinatewise defined linear maps from \(E(X)\) into \(\prod_{n\in\mathbb{N}}X\). In each case where such a truncation is used, the estimates show that it actually takes values in \(E(X)\) and, in fact, defines a bounded operator on \(E(X)\).

Let \(T\colon\ell_{\infty}(X)\to\ell_{\infty}(X)\) be an operator with operator matrix \((T_{n,m})_{n,m\in\mathbb{N}}\). We say that \(T\) acts according to its matrix if, for every \(x=(x_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\in\ell_{\infty}(X)\) and every \(m\in\mathbb{N}\), the series

\(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}T_{m,n}x_{n}\)

norm converges in \(X\) and

\(P_{m}Tx=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}T_{m,n}x_{n}.\)

Let \(T\colon\ell_{\infty}(X)\to\ell_{\infty}(X)\) be an operator, and let \((T_{n,m})_{n,m\in\mathbb{N}}\) be its matrix of. We define the diagonal part \(D\) of \(T\) to be the operator \(D\colon\ell_{\infty}(X)\to\ell_{\infty}(X)\) defined, for each \(x=(x_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\in\ell_{\infty}(X)\) and each \(m\in\mathbb{N}\), by

\(P_{m}Dx=T_{m,m}x_{m}.\)

Similarly, we define the lower triangular part \(L\) of \(T\) to be the operator \(L\colon\ell_{\infty}(X)\to\ell_{\infty}(X)\) defined, for each \(x=(x_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\in\ell_{\infty}(X)\) and each \(m\in\mathbb{N}\), by

\(P_{m}Lx=\sum_{n=1}^{m}T_{m,n}x_{n}.\)

results.title: (Reduction to upper-triangular operators from dual cotype of the dual space).
results.statementHtml:
Let \(X\) be a Banach space such that \(X^{*}\) has finite cotype. Then, for every operator \(T\colon\ell_{1}(X)\to\ell_{1}(X)\) and every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exists an infinite subset \(M\subseteq\mathbb{N}\) such that

\(\|P_{M}TJ_{M}-U\|<\varepsilon,\)

where \(U\colon\ell_{1}(M,X)\to\ell_{1}(M,X)\) is the upper triangular part of \(P_{M}TJ_{M}\).

results.title: (Forward reduction from self-similarity).
results.statementHtml: Let \(E=\ell_{p}\) for \(1<p\leq\infty\) or \(E=c_{0}\), \(X\) and \(Y\) be Banach spaces and \(T\colon E(X)\to\ell_{1}(Y)\) be an operator. Then, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exist a pair of infinite sets \(A,M\subseteq\mathbb{N}\) such that \(\|P_{M}TJ_{A}\|<\varepsilon\).

results.title: (Reduction to upper-triangular operators from self-similarity).
results.statementHtml:
Let \(E=\ell_{p}\) for \(1<p\leq\infty\) or \(E=c_{0}\), \(X\) be a Banach space and \(T\colon\ell_{1}(E(X))\to\ell_{1}(E(X))\) be an operator. Then, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exist an increasing sequence \(\mathbf{n}=(n_{j})_{j\in\mathbb{N}}\) and infinite sets \((A_{j})_{j\in\mathbb{N}}\) so that for all \(j\in\mathbb{N}\) we have

\(\|\widehat{P}_{M_{j}}T\widehat{J}_{n_{j}}J_{A_{j}}\|<\varepsilon/2^{j+1},\)

where \(M_{j}=\{n_{i}:i>j\}\).

results.title: (Forward reduction from cotype).
results.statementHtml:
Let \(X\) be a Banach space with cotype \(q<\infty\), \(E\) denote either \(c_{0}\) or \(\ell_{\infty}\), \(\varepsilon>0\), and \(T\colon\ell_{\infty}^{N}(X)\to E(X)\) be an operator. Denote by \(C_{q}(X)\) the cotype constant of X and suppose that

\(N^{1/q}\varepsilon>2C_{q}(X)\|T\|.\)

Then there exist \(1\leq n\leq N\) and an infinite subset \(M\subseteq\mathbb{N}\) such that

\(\|P_{m}TJ_{n}\|<\varepsilon\qquad\text{for all }m\in M.\)

The point of the previous lemma is not merely the coordinatewise conclusion, but the fact that for \(E=c_{0}\) or \(E=\ell_{\infty}\) one has

\(\|P_{M}TJ_{n}\|=\sup_{m\in M}\|P_{m}TJ_{n}\|.\)

Thus, coordinatewise smallness on \(M\) gives smallness of \(P_{M}TJ_{n}\). Similar coordinatewise forward reductions can be proved for other \(\ell_{p}\)-sums, but they do not by themselves give the required estimate for \(P_{M}TJ_{n}\), since the target norm is no longer a supremum norm.

results.title: (Reduction to upper-triangular operators from cotype).
results.statementHtml:
Let \(E=c_{0}\) or \(E=\ell_{\infty}\), \(X\) be a Banach space with finite cotype, and \(T\colon E(X)\to E(X)\) be an operator. Then, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exists an infinite subset \(M\subseteq\mathbb{N}\) such that, for every \(m\in M\),

\(\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}n<m\\ n\in M\end{subarray}}\|P_{m}TJ_{n}\|<\varepsilon.\)

results.title: (Forward reduction from self-similarity).
results.statementHtml:
Let \(1\leq p<\infty\), \(E=c_{0}\) or \(E=\ell_{\infty}\), \(X\) and \(Y\) be Banach spaces, and \(T\colon\ell_{\infty}^{N}(Y)\to E(\ell_{p}(X))\) be an operator. Suppose that

\(N^{1/p}\varepsilon>2\|T\|.\)

Then there exist \(1\leq n\leq N\), an infinite set \(M\subseteq\mathbb{N}\), and, for each \(m\in M\), an infinite set \(A_{m}\subseteq\mathbb{N}\) such that

\(\|P_{A_{m}}\widehat{P}_{m}TJ_{n}\|<\varepsilon\qquad\text{for all }m\in M.\)

results.title: (Reduction to upper-triangular operators from self-similarity).
results.statementHtml:
Let \(1\leq p<\infty\), \(E=c_{0}\) or \(E=\ell_{\infty}\), \(X\) be a Banach space, and \(T\colon E(\ell_{p}(X))\to E(\ell_{p}(X))\) be an operator. Then, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), there is an infinite set \(M\subseteq\mathbb{N}\) and, for each \(m\in M\), an infinite set \(A_{m}\subseteq\mathbb{N}\) such that

\(\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}n<m\\ n\in M\end{subarray}}\|P_{A_{m}}\widehat{P}_{m}T\widehat{J}_{n}\|<\varepsilon.\)

results.title: (Backward reduction from dual cotype).
results.statementHtml:
Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be Banach spaces, suppose that \(X^{*}\) has cotype \(q<\infty\), and let \(C_{q}(X^{*})\) denote its cotype \(q\) constant. Let \(\varepsilon>0\) and \(T\colon X\to\ell_{1}^{N}(Y)\) be an operator. Suppose that

\(N^{1/q}\varepsilon>2C_{q}(X^{*})\|T\|.\)

Then there exists \(1\leq n\leq N\) such that

\(\|P_{n}T\|<\varepsilon.\)

The reason this reduction is effective for \(\ell_{1}\)-sums is that restrictions to coordinate sets are controlled by the individual coordinate restrictions. Indeed, if \(S\colon\ell_{1}(X)\to Y\) is bounded and \(M\subseteq\mathbb{N}\), then

\(\|SJ_{M}\|=\sup_{m\in M}\|SJ_{m}\|.\)

Hence, coordinatewise smallness on \(M\) immediately yields smallness of the restricted operator \(SJ_{M}\). One may prove analogous coordinatewise backward reductions for other \(\ell_{p}\)-sums, but such estimates no longer control \(SJ_{M}\) itself, since the domain norm is not the \(\ell_{1}\)-norm.

results.title: (Reduction to lower-triangular operators from dual cotype).
results.statementHtml:
Let \(X\) be a Banach space such that \(X^{*}\) has finite cotype. Then, for every operator \(T\colon\ell_{1}(X)\to\ell_{1}(X)\) and every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exists an infinite subset \(M\subseteq\mathbb{N}\) such that

\(\|P_{M}TJ_{M}-L\|<\varepsilon,\)

where \(L\colon\ell_{1}(M,X)\to\ell_{1}(M,X)\) is the lower triangular part of \(P_{M}TJ_{M}\).

results.title: (Backward reduction from self-similarity).
results.statementHtml:
Let \(1<p<\infty\), \(X\) and \(Y\) be Banach spaces, \(\varepsilon>0\), and \(T\colon\ell_{p}(X)\to\ell_{1}^{N}(Y)\) be an operator. Suppose that

\(N^{(p-1)/p}\varepsilon>2\|T\|.\)

Then there exists \(1\leq n\leq N\) and \(M\subseteq\mathbb{N}\) infinite such that

\(\|P_{n}TJ_{M}\|<\varepsilon.\)

The same result holds for operators from \(c_{0}(X)\) and \(\ell_{\infty}(X)\) provided \(N\varepsilon>2\|T\|\).

results.title: (Reduction to lower-triangular operators from self-similarity).
results.statementHtml:
Let \(E=\ell_{p}\) for \(1<p\leq\infty\) or \(E=c_{0}\), \(X\) be a Banach space and \(T\colon\ell_{1}(E(X))\to\ell_{1}(E(X))\) be an operator. Then, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exist an increasing sequence \(\mathbf{n}=(n_{j})_{j\in\mathbb{N}}\) and infinite sets \((A_{j})_{j\in\mathbb{N}}\) so that for all \(i\in\mathbb{N}\) we have that whenever \(j>i\) then

\(\|\widehat{P}_{n_{i}}T\widehat{J}_{n_{j}}J_{A_{j}}\|<\varepsilon/2^{i+1}.\)

results.title: (Backward reduction from cotype).
results.statementHtml: Let \(X\) have cotype \(q<\infty\), \(E\) be either \(c_{0}\) or \(\ell_{\infty}\), and \(T\colon E(X)\to X\) be an operator. Then, for every \(\varepsilon>0\) there exists an infinite subset \(M\subseteq\mathbb{N}\) such that \(\|TJ_{M}\|<\varepsilon\).

results.title: (Reduction to lower-triangular operators from cotype).
results.statementHtml:
Let \(X\) be a Banach space with finite cotype \(q\), \(E=c_{0}\) or \(E=\ell_{\infty}\) and \(T:E(X)\to E(X)\) be an operator. Then for every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exists an infinite subset \(M\subseteq\mathbb{N}\) such that

\(\|P_{M}TJ_{M}-L\|<\varepsilon,\)

where \(L\colon E(M,X)\to E(M,X)\) is the lower triangular part of \(P_{M}TJ_{M}\).

results.title: (Backward reduction from self-similarity).
results.statementHtml: Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be Banach spaces, \(E=c_{0}\) or \(E=\ell_{\infty}\) and \(T\colon E(Y)\to\ell_{p}(X)\) be an operator where \(1\leq p<\infty\). Then for any \(\varepsilon>0\), there exist infinite sets \(A,M\subseteq\mathbb{N}\) such that \(\|P_{A}TJ_{M}\|<\varepsilon\).

results.title: (Reduction to lower-triangular operators from self-similarity).
results.statementHtml:
Let \(1\leq p<\infty\), \(E=c_{0}\) or \(E=\ell_{\infty}\), \(X\) be a Banach space, and \(T\colon E(\ell_{p}(X))\to E(\ell_{p}(X))\) be an operator. Then, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exists an infinite set \(M\subseteq\mathbb{N}\) and, for each \(m\in M\), an infinite set \(A_{m}\subseteq\mathbb{N}\) such that, for every \(m\in M\),

\(\|P_{A_{m}}\widehat{P}_{m}T\widehat{J}_{M_{m}}\|<\varepsilon,\)

where \(M_{m}=\{n\in M:n>m\}\).

results.title: (Diagonal reduction from dual cotype).
results.statementHtml:
Let \(X\) be a Banach space such that \(X^{*}\) has finite cotype, and let \(T\colon\ell_{1}(X)\to\ell_{1}(X)\) be an operator. Then, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exists an infinite subset \(M\subseteq\mathbb{N}\) such that

\(\|P_{M}TJ_{M}-D\|<\varepsilon,\)

where \(D\colon\ell_{1}(M,X)\to\ell_{1}(M,X)\) is the diagonal part of \(P_{M}TJ_{M}\).

results.title: (Diagonal reduction from self-similarity).
results.statementHtml:
Let \(E=\ell_{p}\) for \(1<p\leq\infty\) or \(E=c_{0}\) and \(T\colon\ell_{1}(E(X))\to\ell_{1}(E(X))\) be an operator. Then, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exist infinite increasing sequences \(\mathbf{n}=(n_{j})_{j\in\mathbb{N}}\) and \(\mathbf{m}=(m_{j})_{j\in\mathbb{N}}\) such that

\(\|P_{\mathbf{n},\mathbf{m}}TJ_{\mathbf{n},\mathbf{m}}-D\|<\varepsilon,\)

where \(D\colon\ell_{1}(X)\to\ell_{1}(X)\) is the diagonal part of \(P_{\mathbf{n},\mathbf{m}}TJ_{\mathbf{n},\mathbf{m}}\).

results.title: (Diagonal reduction from cotype).
results.statementHtml:
Let \(X\) be a Banach space with finite cotype, \(E=c_{0}\) or \(E=\ell_{\infty}\), and \(T\colon E(X)\to E(X)\) be an operator. Then, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exists an infinite subset \(M\subseteq\mathbb{N}\) such that

\(\|P_{M}TJ_{M}-D\|<\varepsilon,\)

where \(D\colon E(M,X)\to E(M,X)\) is the diagonal part of \(P_{M}TJ_{M}\).

results.title: (Diagonal reduction from self-similarity).
results.statementHtml:
Let \(1\leq p<\infty\), \(E=c_{0}\) or \(E=\ell_{\infty}\), \(X\) be a Banach space, and \(T\colon E(\ell_{p}(X))\to E(\ell_{p}(X))\) be an operator. Then, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exist increasing sequences \(\mathbf{n}=(n_{j})_{j\in\mathbb{N}}\) and \(\mathbf{m}=(m_{j})_{j\in\mathbb{N}}\) such that

\(\|P_{\mathbf{n},\mathbf{m}}TJ_{\mathbf{n},\mathbf{m}}-D\|<\varepsilon,\)

where \(D\colon E(X)\to E(X)\) is the diagonal part of \(P_{\mathbf{n},\mathbf{m}}TJ_{\mathbf{n},\mathbf{m}}\).

Let \(E=\ell_{1}\), \(E=\ell_{\infty}\), or \(E=c_{0}\), and \(X\) be a Banach space with the \(C\)-PFP. Then, for every diagonal operator \(D\colon E(X)\to E(X)\), either \(D\) or \(I_{E(X)}-D\) factors the identity on \(E(X)\) with constant \(C\).

results.title: (Stability of factorisation under perturbations).
results.statementHtml:
Let \(X\) be a Banach space and \(T,S\in\mathscr{B}(X)\). Suppose that \(T\) factors the identity on \(X\) with constant \(C\) and that

\(C\|S-T\|<1/2.\)

Then \(S\) factors the identity on \(X\) with constant \(2C\).

results.title: (Capon localisation).
results.statementHtml:
Let \(S\colon L_{1}[0,1]\to L_{1}[0,1]\) be an operator, and let \((\nu_{t})_{t\in[0,1]}\) be the family of measures associated with \(S\) by Kalton’s representation theorem. Suppose that, for some \(a>0\), the set

\(E_{a}(S)=\{t\in[0,1]:|\nu_{t}(\{t\})|>a\}\)

has positive measure. Then, for every \(0<\varepsilon<a\), there is a measurable set \(A\subseteq[0,1]\) of positive measure such that, whenever \(B\subseteq A\) has positive measure, the operator

\(M_{B}S\jmath_{B}\colon L_{1}(B)\to L_{1}(B)\)

is an isomorphism onto \(L_{1}(B)\), and

\(\|M_{B}S\jmath_{B}f\|\geq(a-\varepsilon)\|f\|\qquad(f\in L_{1}(B)).\)

Consequently,

\(\|(M_{B}S\jmath_{B})^{-1}\|\leq\frac{1}{a-\varepsilon}.\)
The space \(L_{1}[0,1]\) has the UPFP.

results.title: (Finite interference).
results.statementHtml:
Let \(\Lambda\) be a set and \(S\colon L_{1}[0,1]\to\ell_{1}(\Lambda,L_{1}[0,1])\) be an operator. Then, for every \(\eta>0\), there are a finite set \(F\subseteq\Lambda\) and a measurable set \(B\subseteq[0,1]\) of positive measure such that

\(\|P_{\Lambda\setminus F}S\jmath_{B}\|<\eta.\)

results.title: (Finite free set).
results.statementHtml:
Let \(\Gamma\) be an uncountable set, and let \(F_{\gamma}\subseteq\Gamma\setminus\{\gamma\}\) be finite for each \(\gamma\in\Gamma\). Then there is a set \(H\subseteq\Gamma\) such that \(|H|=|\Gamma|\) and, for every \(\gamma\in H\), we have

\(F_{\gamma}\cap H=\varnothing.\)

results.title: (Diagonal reduction).
results.statementHtml:
Let \(\Gamma\) be an uncountable set, and let \(T\colon\ell_{1}(\Gamma,L_{1}[0,1])\to\ell_{1}(\Gamma,L_{1}[0,1])\) be an operator. Then, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), there are a set \(H\subseteq\Gamma\) with \(|H|=|\Gamma|\), measurable sets \(B_{\gamma}\subseteq[0,1]\) of positive measure for \(\gamma\in H\), contractions

\(V\colon\left(\bigoplus_{\gamma\in H}L_{1}(B_{\gamma})\right)_{\ell_{1}}\to\ell_{1}(H,L_{1}[0,1])\)

and

\(U\colon\ell_{1}(H,L_{1}[0,1])\to\left(\bigoplus_{\gamma\in H}L_{1}(B_{\gamma})\right)_{\ell_{1}}\)

such that

\(UV=I_{\bigl(\bigoplus_{\gamma\in H}L_{1}(B_{\gamma})\bigr)_{\ell_{1}}},\)

and a diagonal operator \(D\) on \(\bigl(\bigoplus_{\gamma\in H}L_{1}(B_{\gamma})\bigr)_{\ell_{1}}\) such that

\(\|UP_{H}TJ_{H}V-D\|\leq\varepsilon.\)

results.title: (Diagonal dichotomy).
results.statementHtml:
Let \(C\geq 1\), let \(H\) be an uncountable set, and for each \(\alpha\in H\) let \(B_{\alpha}\subseteq[0,1]\) be measurable with positive measure. Suppose that \(L_{1}[0,1]\) has the \(C\)-PFP. Put

\(Y=\left(\bigoplus_{\alpha\in H}L_{1}(B_{\alpha})\right)_{\ell_{1}}.\)

Then, for every diagonal operator \(D\colon Y\to Y\), either \(D\) or \(I_{Y}-D\) factors the identity on \(Y\) with constant \(C\).
Let \(1<p<\infty\). Are there natural and sufficiently broad conditions on a Banach space \(X\) under which the UPFP of \(X\) passes to \(\ell_{p}(X)\)?

In the uncountable setting, the need for a full two-sided reduction can sometimes be avoided. Indeed, once a one-sided finite-interference estimate is available, Hajnal’s free set theorem can remove the finitely many exceptional coordinates on a large subset of the index set. Thus the cotype and self-similarity mechanisms used in the countable reductions above are expected to give corresponding UPFP results for uncountable sums \(\ell_{p}(\Gamma,X)\), \(1<p<\infty\), under the analogous hypotheses.
Is there a Banach space \(X\) with the PFP, respectively the UPFP, such that \(\ell_{p}(X)\), for some \(1\leq p\leq\infty\), or \(c_{0}(X)\) fails the PFP, respectively the UPFP?
Is there a primary Banach space \(X\) such that \(\ell_{p}(X)\), for some \(1\leq p\leq\infty\), or \(c_{0}(X)\) is not primary?

theorem-1-1.note: If a Banach space X has UPFP and either X is isomorphic to ell_p(X) for some 1<=p<=infinity or to c0(X), or X* has finite cotype, then ell_1(X) has UPFP and is primary. Completeness is an explicit binder. The two alternatives are a disjunction, and cotype concerns the actual bounded linear dual. The self-similarity quantifier includes p=1 and p=infinity and the separate c0 alternative. Both conclusions are retained.

theorem-1-2.note: If a Banach space X has UPFP and either X is isomorphic to ell_p(X) for some finite p>=1 or X has finite cotype, then both c0(X) and ell_infinity(X) have UPFP and both are primary. Finite-p self-similarity explicitly excludes infinity and has no c0 branch. Cotype is on X, not its dual. There are four conclusions. c0(X) is the genuine continuous-at-infinity space C0(N,X); the natural numbers carry their discrete topology.

corollary-1-3.note: For every finite p>=1, ell_infinity(Lp[0,1]) has UPFP and is primary. Also c0(L1[0,1]) has UPFP and is primary. All finite exponents are quantified. Lp is the a.e.-quotient space for Lebesgue measure restricted to [0,1], with the actual Lp norm. The additional c0(L1) claim is a separate conjunction, not omitted or restricted to p>1.

remark-1-4.note: This passage is explanatory. No separate theorem certificate is attached to it.

corollary-1-5.note: For every ordinal alpha, ell_1(C([0,alpha])) has UPFP and is primary. No countability, regularity or non-exceptional-ordinal hypothesis is added. The printed exception split belongs in the proof, not in the target. Numbering includes the intervening Remark 1.4.

theorem-1-6.note: For every set Gamma, ell_1(Gamma,L1[0,1]) has UPFP. Consequently C[0,1]* has UPFP and is primary. Gamma is an arbitrary type in an arbitrary universe, with no nonemptiness, countability or cardinal-arithmetic hypothesis. All three original claims are retained, including both real and complex scalars. Empty indices are handled separately inside the proof.
